edges.effect_quant: Across cardiac populations, high-intensity interval training improved peak VO2 more than moderate continuous training by about 1.76 mL/kg/min, and post-MI reviews generally place the benefit on the same side even when early application remains more cautious.
edges.population: stable adults in cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction
edges.mechanism: Interval-based training can deliver a higher cardiorespiratory stimulus within a tolerable session load, promoting greater peak oxygen uptake gains than steady moderate exercise. In post-MI rehabilitation, that advantage depends on patient stability and careful supervision early after infarction.
edges.summary: The clearest evidence is the broader cardiac meta-analysis showing that interval training raises peak VO2 more than moderate continuous training. MI-specific synthesis and the HIIT-EARLY trial point in the same direction for fitness, but they also show why this is not a universal one-size-fits-all prescription immediately after infarction. The edge is best viewed as protective for VO2max in appropriately selected post-MI patients.
edges.caveats: Most trials enrolled clinically stable and relatively low-risk participants, so these findings should not be generalized to frail or unstable post-MI populations. The advantage is more consistent for fitness outcomes than for hard clinical outcomes or remodeling endpoints.
